c10_phy_ch01.title: Electricity
c10_phy_ch01.subtitle: Build circuits, measure current, and learn why your house wiring is designed the way it is.
c10_phy_ch01.role: an apprentice electrician checking a newly wired room
c10_phy_ch01.intro: A house has tripped its breaker three times this week. Your job: find what's wrong with the circuit logic before anyone touches a wire.
c10_phy_ch01.goal: Predict current, voltage and resistance in any circuit you build — and explain why series and parallel behave so differently.

discovery.question: Two identical bulbs — one wired in series, one in parallel. Which setup glows brighter, and why does the answer surprise most people?
options: Parallel — each bulb gets the full voltage
Series — the current is stronger
They glow the same — bulbs are identical
Series — the voltage adds up
discovery.answer: Parallel — each bulb gets the full voltage
discovery.hook: Most students think 'more components = more power'. In series the current must fight through both bulbs — parallel gives each its own path.

c10_phy_ch01.mission: On the circuit lab: build a series and a parallel circuit — measure what happens to brightness when you remove one bulb from each.
c10_phy_ch01.finale: Ohm's law isn't a formula to memorise — it's the reason your house is wired in parallel and why a fuse is a calculated sacrifice.

c10_phy_ch04.title: Light: Reflection and Refraction
c10_phy_ch04.subtitle: Bend light with lenses and mirrors until you can predict exactly where the image lands.
c10_phy_ch04.intro: A patient can't read the board past 3 metres. Before you grind a single lens, you need to know exactly what shape bends light back onto the retina.
c10_phy_ch04.goal: Trace rays through any lens or mirror — predict image position, size and whether it's real or virtual.

discovery.question: A spoon in a glass of water looks bent at the waterline. The spoon is perfectly straight — so what actually changed?
options: Light changed speed crossing air to water, so its path bent
Water magnifies the spoon
The glass distorts the image
Reflection off the water surface doubles it
discovery.answer: Light changed speed crossing air to water, so its path bent
discovery.hook: The bend isn't an illusion of the glass — light literally slows down in water, and changing speed means changing direction.

c10_phy_ch04.mission: On the lens lab: move the object from beyond 2F to between F and the lens — watch the image flip from real-and-shrinking to virtual-and-magnified.
c10_phy_ch04.finale: Every camera, telescope, microscope and pair of spectacles is one idea: light obeys rules, and rules can be bent into instruments.

c10_chem_ch01.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
c10_chem_ch01.subtitle: Learn to read reactions like sentences — and balance them so no atom goes missing.
c10_chem_ch01.role: a lab chemist documenting an experiment
c10_chem_ch01.intro: Your iron nail left in copper sulphate turned coppery brown overnight. Your job: write the equation that explains where the copper came from.
c10_chem_ch01.goal: Identify reaction types on sight and balance any equation without losing an atom.

discovery.question: You burn 10g of magnesium and the ash weighs MORE than 10g. Where did the extra mass come from?
options: Oxygen from the air joined the magnesium
Burning creates matter
The scale is wrong
Heat adds weight
discovery.answer: Oxygen from the air joined the magnesium
discovery.hook: Most students think burning makes things disappear. Mass is never created or destroyed — the missing mass was in the air all along.

c10_chem_ch01.mission: Balance three equations in the lab — start with the unbalanced skeleton and place coefficients until every atom counts.
c10_chem_ch01.finale: A balanced equation is a promise: atoms are never lost, only rearranged. Every industry from steel to medicine runs on that promise.

c10_bio_ch03.title: How Do Organisms Reproduce
c10_bio_ch03.subtitle: From cell division to fertilisation — how life copies itself, and why it never copies perfectly.
c10_bio_ch03.role: a plant breeder developing a new variety
c10_bio_ch03.intro: You have a rose that flowers brilliantly but never sets seed. Your job: decide whether to propagate it asexually or cross it — and what each choice does to variation.
c10_bio_ch03.goal: Compare asexual and sexual reproduction — and explain why variation is survival's insurance policy.

discovery.question: A single bacterium becomes a billion identical copies overnight — yet a species of bacteria can still out-evolve antibiotics. Where does the variation come from?
options: Mutation during copying — imperfect division creates differences
They reproduce sexually too
The antibiotic creates the variation
Variation only happens in animals
discovery.answer: Mutation during copying — imperfect division creates differences
discovery.hook: Most students think asexual copies are always identical. Copying billions of times means billions of chances to be slightly different.

c10_bio_ch03.mission: On the reproduction lab: run one asexual cycle and one sexual cycle — count how much variation each produces.
c10_bio_ch03.finale: Reproduction is life's way of saying: copy yourself, but not perfectly — the imperfections are how species survive what they can't predict.

c10_bio_ch04.title: Heredity and Evolution
c10_bio_ch04.subtitle: Why you have your grandmother's eyes — and how small changes over millennia built every species alive.
c10_bio_ch04.role: a genetic counsellor explaining a family trait
c10_bio_ch04.intro: A couple asks why their child has a trait neither parent shows. Your job: trace the recessive allele that hid for a generation.
c10_bio_ch04.goal: Predict trait inheritance with Punnett logic and explain how selection turns small variations into new species.

discovery.question: Two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child. Neither parent's eyes are blue — so whose eyes did the child inherit?
options: Both parents carried a hidden blue-eye gene
A grandparent's gene skipped generations
The mutation happened at birth
Eye colour isn't inherited
discovery.answer: Both parents carried a hidden blue-eye gene
discovery.hook: Recessive traits don't vanish — they hide. Two carriers can both look one way while silently carrying the other.

c10_bio_ch04.mission: On the heredity lab: cross two heterozygous parents and watch the 3:1 ratio emerge from hundreds of offspring.
c10_bio_ch04.finale: You are the running total of every inheritance since life began — heredity explains your eyes, and evolution explains why eyes exist at all.

c9_physics_ch02.title: Motion
c9_physics_ch02.subtitle: Distance, displacement, speed, velocity — the vocabulary that turns 'it moved' into physics.
c9_physics_ch02.role: a sports analyst timing a sprinter
c9_physics_ch02.intro: Two runners finish 100m together — but one's speed graph tells a completely different story. Your job: read the graph and find who actually ran faster when.
c9_physics_ch02.goal: Read and build distance-time and velocity-time graphs — extract speed, acceleration and displacement on sight.

discovery.question: You drive 40 km to school and back home. Odometer says 80 km. A physicist says your displacement is zero. Who's right?
options: Both — displacement measures position change, not travel
The odometer — distance is what matters
The physicist — the trip was wasted
Neither — displacement is always half the distance
discovery.answer: Both — displacement measures position change, not travel
discovery.hook: Distance and displacement are different questions — one asks 'how far did you travel', the other 'how far did you end up'.

c9_physics_ch02.mission: On the motion lab: draw a velocity-time graph for a car that speeds up, cruises, and brakes — read the displacement from the area.
c9_physics_ch02.finale: Graphs are where motion becomes readable — every GPS, every crash test, every rocket trajectory is a story told in slopes and areas.

c9_physics_ch03.title: Force and Laws of Motion
c9_physics_ch03.subtitle: Inertia, momentum and action-reaction — Newton's three laws run every collision from cricket to car crashes.
c9_physics_ch03.role: a crash-test engineer analysing an impact
c9_physics_ch03.intro: Two test cars collide — one heavier, one faster. Your job: use momentum to predict which dummy gets hurt before the crash happens.
c9_physics_ch03.goal: Apply all three laws to real collisions — calculate momentum, feel inertia, predict reaction forces.

discovery.question: A tablecloth is yanked out from under a full dinner setting — and the plates barely move. What law just saved dinner?
options: Inertia — objects resist changes to their state of rest
Friction held the plates
The cloth was too smooth to matter
Gravity pinned them down
discovery.answer: Inertia — objects resist changes to their state of rest
discovery.hook: The plates didn't 'stay' — they simply refused to start moving. Newton's first law: stillness is also a state that takes a force to change.

c9_physics_ch03.mission: On the collision lab: vary mass and velocity, measure momentum before and after — verify it never disappears.
c9_physics_ch03.finale: Seatbelts, airbags, rocket launches, every cricket shot — three sentences Newton wrote in 1687 are still running all of it.

c9_math_ch03.title: Number Systems
c9_math_ch03.subtitle: From counting numbers to irrationals — the number line is bigger than it looks.
c9_math_ch03.intro: A colleague claims every number on the line is a fraction in disguise. Your job: find the number that proves him wrong.
c9_math_ch03.goal: Classify any number — natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational — and prove why √2 can't be a fraction.

discovery.question: Between any two fractions there's always another fraction. So is EVERY number a fraction?
options: No — √2 and π can never be written as fractions
Yes — decimals are just fractions in disguise
Yes — infinity means every number is rational
No — only negatives aren't fractions
discovery.answer: No — √2 and π can never be written as fractions
discovery.hook: The number line looks complete with fractions — but irrationals fill gaps the rationals can't touch.

c9_math_ch03.mission: On the number line: locate √2 by geometry — construct it, and see exactly where it sits between the rationals.
c9_math_ch03.finale: Number systems are humanity expanding what 'number' means — every extension was once heresy and is now arithmetic.

c6_physics_ch03.title: Electricity: Circuits and Components
c6_physics_ch03.subtitle: Your first real circuits — make a bulb glow, break it, and learn why.
c6_physics_ch03.role: a young inventor fixing a torch
c6_physics_ch03.intro: Your torch went dark at the worst moment. Battery's fine, bulb's fine — so what part of the loop gave up?
c6_physics_ch03.goal: Build working circuits from cells, wires and bulbs — and know why a circuit must be a complete loop.

discovery.question: A torch has a battery and a working bulb but won't light. What's the most likely reason?
options: The circuit isn't a complete loop — current needs a path back
The battery is always the problem
Bulbs need two batteries
Torches need sunlight first
discovery.answer: The circuit isn't a complete loop — current needs a path back
discovery.hook: Electricity can't travel one way — it needs a circle. Break the circle anywhere and everything stops.

c6_physics_ch03.mission: On the circuit board: complete the loop to light the bulb — then break it in three different places and predict what happens each time.
c6_physics_ch03.finale: You just learned the rule every electrician lives by: current only flows in complete loops. Every switch, fuse and plug is a controlled way to open or close one.

c6_math_ch05.title: Algebra
c6_math_ch05.subtitle: Letters that stand for numbers — the first time maths learns to talk about the unknown.
c6_math_ch05.role: a codebreaker finding a hidden number
c6_math_ch05.intro: A puzzle says: 'I think of a number, double it, add 6, get 20.' Your job: find the number without guessing.
c6_math_ch05.goal: Turn word puzzles into equations and solve for the unknown — forwards and backwards.

discovery.question: I think of a number, add 5, and get 12. You don't know my number — but can you still find it?
options: Yes — work backwards: 12 minus 5 is 7
No — you can't solve what you can't see
Only by guessing every number
Yes — but only if the number is even
discovery.hook: Algebra's superpower: you don't need to see the number — the equation sees it for you.

c6_math_ch05.mission: On the balance: keep both sides equal while you undo the operations — that's literally what solving an equation is.
c6_math_ch05.finale: Every unknown you'll ever solve — in science, money, code — is just a letter standing in until you work backwards to find it.

c11_phy_ch03.title: Motion in a Plane
c11_phy_ch03.subtitle: Two dimensions change everything — projectiles, vectors, and why the fastest path isn't a straight line.
c11_phy_ch03.role: a basketball physicist perfecting a three-pointer
c11_phy_ch03.intro: The shot leaves your hands at 45°. Your job: find the launch angle that maximises range — and explain why it isn't 90°.
c11_phy_ch03.goal: Resolve vectors, predict projectile paths, and understand why horizontal and vertical motion are independent.

discovery.question: A ball thrown straight up from a moving truck lands... where? Most people say 'behind the truck' — what does physics say?
options: Back in your hand — it keeps the truck's horizontal speed
Behind the truck
Straight down where it was thrown
It depends on the wind
discovery.answer: Back in your hand — it keeps the truck's horizontal speed
discovery.hook: The ball never forgets it was moving with you. Horizontal and vertical motion are separate stories told at the same time.

c11_phy_ch03.mission: On the projectile lab: launch at 30°, 45°, 60° — measure range and air time, and find the angle that wins.
c11_phy_ch03.finale: Every cricket throw, every long jump, every water fountain is the same two independent motions — you can now see them separately.

c11_phy_ch05.title: Work, Energy and Power
c11_phy_ch05.subtitle: The physics of getting things done — and why holding a heavy bag still isn't 'work' at all.
c11_phy_ch05.role: a ride designer rating a roller coaster
c11_phy_ch05.intro: Your coaster car must clear the second hill using only the energy from the first drop. Your job: check the energy math before anyone rides.
c11_phy_ch05.goal: Track energy as it converts — kinetic to potential and back — and compute real work and power.

discovery.question: You stand still holding a 10 kg bag for an hour. Exhausted — but a physicist says you did ZERO work on the bag. How?
options: No displacement = no work, however tired you feel
The bag was too light to count
You did work — the physicist is wrong
Only machines do work
discovery.answer: No displacement = no work, however tired you feel
discovery.hook: Physics defines work as force × displacement — your muscles burned energy fighting your own cells, not moving the bag.

c11_phy_ch05.mission: On the energy track: drop the car from different heights and measure speed at the bottom — verify mgh really does become ½mv².
c11_phy_ch05.finale: Energy is the universe's currency — it never appears or disappears, only changes hands. Roller coasters, dams and your breakfast all run on the same ledger.

c11_bio_ch08.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
c11_bio_ch08.subtitle: Shrink to the scale where everything alive is made of the same basic machine.
c11_bio_ch08.role: a microscopist on their first day in a research lab
c11_bio_ch08.intro: Under the lens, a plant cell and a cheek cell look like different worlds — and run on the same parts list. Your job: map what's inside.
c11_bio_ch08.goal: Identify every organelle, what it does, and what breaks when it fails.

discovery.question: Your body makes ~2 million new cells every second — yet you stay 'you'. What keeps billions of divisions faithful?
options: DNA inside each cell carries the same instructions
Cells copy from a master template stored in the brain
The body replaces mistakes instantly
Cells don't actually copy — they grow
discovery.answer: DNA inside each cell carries the same instructions
discovery.hook: Every cell carries the full instruction set — fidelity isn't enforced from outside, it's written into every copy.

c11_bio_ch08.mission: On the cell explorer: zoom into a cell and identify organelles by function — which one makes energy? which packages proteins?
c11_bio_ch08.finale: You're a colony of 37 trillion specialists — every organelle you just met is a worker keeping you alive right now.

c12_bio_ch08.title: Human Health and Disease
c12_bio_ch08.subtitle: How your immune system hunts, remembers, and sometimes turns on itself.
c12_bio_ch08.intro: A measles case appears in a school that dropped vaccination rates. Your job: explain why one case can become twenty — and why vaccinated kids protect the unvaccinated.
c12_bio_ch08.goal: Trace how pathogens spread, how immunity works, and why herd immunity is a community property.

discovery.question: You get a vaccine that's a harmless piece of the virus — and become immune to the real thing. What did your body actually learn?
options: To recognize the invader's shape — memory cells keep the photo
To kill all viruses forever
To build walls around cells
The vaccine does the fighting itself
discovery.answer: To recognize the invader's shape — memory cells keep the photo
discovery.hook: Vaccines don't fight the disease — they teach your immune system what it looks like, so the real fight is won before it starts.

c12_bio_ch08.mission: On the immune lab: introduce a pathogen, watch the first response — then reintroduce it and watch memory cells answer in hours, not days.
c12_bio_ch08.finale: Immunity is memory you didn't know you had — every cold you fought is recorded, and every vaccine is a wanted poster your cells already have.

c12_phy_ch06.title: Electromagnetic Induction
c12_phy_ch06.subtitle: The discovery that powers the grid — motion becoming electricity.
c12_phy_ch06.role: a power-grid engineer designing a generator
c12_phy_ch06.intro: A city needs electricity that doesn't come from batteries. Your job: figure out how moving a magnet near a coil creates current from nothing.
c12_phy_ch06.goal: Predict when induction happens, which way current flows, and why changing flux is everything.

discovery.question: A magnet sits perfectly still inside a coil — nothing happens. Move it, and current flows. Where does the electricity come from?
options: The changing magnetic field — motion is the source
The magnet contains charge that jumps
The coil stores static from the air
Friction between magnet and coil
discovery.answer: The changing magnetic field — motion is the source
discovery.hook: A still magnet creates nothing — induction needs change. It's not the field that generates current; it's the field CHANGING.

c12_phy_ch06.mission: On the induction lab: move the magnet faster and slower — watch how the current tracks the RATE of change, not the position.
c12_phy_ch06.finale: Faraday moved a magnet in a coil and lit the world — every generator in every dam, coal plant and wind farm is still running his experiment.

c8_math_ch05.title: Number Play
c8_math_ch05.subtitle: Divisibility tricks, digit puzzles, and why some numbers hide patterns in plain sight.
c8_math_ch05.intro: A friend claims they can tell instantly whether any number divides by 9 — without dividing. Your job: find their trick, then prove it always works.
c8_math_ch05.goal: Use digit patterns and place value to explain divisibility rules — not just apply them.

discovery.question: Take any 3-digit number, reverse it, subtract the smaller from the larger — the answer is ALWAYS divisible by 99. Coincidence?
options: No — place value forces the difference to be 99 times a digit gap
Yes — a numerical coincidence
Only for certain numbers
Only if the digits are different
discovery.answer: No — place value forces the difference to be 99 times a digit gap
discovery.hook: The trick isn't magic — it's place value. abc − cba = 99(a−c), always. The digits decide everything.

c8_math_ch05.mission: Test the rule yourself: try five different numbers — then figure out WHY it must always work.
c8_math_ch05.finale: Number patterns are arithmetic wearing a costume — learn to see the structure and 'tricks' become proofs.
